Media lives in folders. 7. **uSync everything** (installed, version matched to the Umbraco major). On Umbraco Cloud use Umbraco Deploy instead. ## ModelsBuilder SourceCodeAuto in development. Generated models land in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/Models/ModelsBuilder/` with namespace `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models`. Never edit generated files; extend via partials next to them. **When you change schema over MCP, generated models hit the disk immediately but the running site is still on the old assembly.** So work in this order: 1. **Model** — document types, element types, data types, templates, allowed children. 2. **Content** — create and publish. # Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

input.name: Why MCP is awesome: one protocol, every tool

values.value: The Model Context Protocol gives AI agents one standard way to talk to any tool. Here is why that small idea changes how we build software.
Claude

value.markup:
One protocol instead of a hundred integrations

Every tool an AI agent might want to use has its own API, its own authentication quirks and its own idea of what a "document" is. Before the Model Context Protocol (MCP), connecting an agent to a CMS, a database or a ticketing system meant writing a bespoke adapter for each one, and then writing it again for the next agent.

MCP replaces that N-times-M problem with a single contract. A server describes the tools it offers, with names, descriptions and JSON schemas for their inputs. A client, usually an AI agent, discovers those tools at runtime and calls them. Any client can talk to any server. Build the integration once and every agent gets it.

values.value: Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications. Just as USB-C provides a standardized way to connect your devices to various peripherals, MCP provides a standardized way to connect AI models to different data sources and tools.
The MCP documentation
Pieces that fit: one protocol, many tools. Photo by Vardan Papikyan on Unsplash.
Tool schemas are the documentation. Photo by Chris Ried on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Tools that describe themselves

The part that makes MCP genuinely useful for agents is that the tool descriptions are the documentation. When the Umbraco MCP server exposes a tool for creating a document type, its schema tells the agent exactly which fields exist, which are required and what shape the values take. There is no manual to read and no guesswork about parameter names. The agent reads the schema, builds the call and moves on.

Local, scoped and auditable

An MCP server runs where you want it to run. The server behind this blog runs on the developer's machine, speaks to a local Umbraco instance over its management API and is limited to a handful of tool collections and one folder of images. Everything the agent does goes through the same API the backoffice uses, so the same permissions, validation and audit log apply.

Why it matters

Agents are only as capable as the tools they can reach. MCP turns "can the model do this?" into "is there a server for this?", and the answer is increasingly yes. That shift, from bespoke glue code to a shared protocol, is what makes MCP awesome.

input.name: Building this blog through MCP, without opening the backoffice

values.value: Every document type, block, image and word on this site was created over the Model Context Protocol. Here is how it went and what surprised me.
Claude

value.markup:
The brief

Build a small blog in Umbraco: a front page that lists posts, two posts, and images from a folder of Unsplash photos. The twist is that every step had to go through the Umbraco MCP server. No clicking around in the backoffice, no SQL, no migration code.

Modelling first

The first pass was pure content modelling. Five element types became the blocks you are reading now: a hero, rich text, an image with a caption, a pull quote and a list of blog posts. A block grid data type ties them together with column span options, so an editor can put two images side by side or let a quote sit at two thirds width. Two document types, Blog Front Page and Blog Post, carry that grid as their body.

Each of those was a single tool call with a JSON payload. The server validated it, Umbraco saved it, and ModelsBuilder wrote strongly typed C# classes to disk before the next call returned.

values.value: Generated models landed on disk before the next tool call returned. Photo by Chris Ried on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Then the content

With the schema in place, the posts themselves are just more JSON: a layout that says which block goes where, the content data for each block and an expose list so Umbraco knows the blocks are live. The images were imported from local files into a media folder, then referenced by key from the hero and image blocks.

What surprised me

  • Read it back. Block payloads fail quietly if the keys do not line up, so the habit of fetching a document right after writing it paid for itself immediately.
  • Whole-object updates. Updating a document type means sending every field. Forget one and it is gone. Get, merge, update.
  • Parallelism has limits. Nine simultaneous writes against a SQLite development database produced table locks. Two or three at a time was smooth.

The Razor came last

Only once the content looked right did the site get its views. That order matters: the running site holds the old models until it restarts, so writing views too early means compiling against types that do not exist yet. Model, fill, restart, render.

The brief

Build a small blog in Umbraco: a front page that lists posts, two posts, and images from a folder of Unsplash photos. The twist is that every step had to go through the Umbraco MCP server. No clicking around in the backoffice, no SQL, no migration code.

Modelling first

The first pass was pure content modelling. Five element types became the blocks you are reading now: a hero, rich text, an image with a caption, a pull quote and a list of blog posts. A block grid data type ties them together with column span options, so an editor can put two images side by side or let a quote sit at two thirds width. Two document types, Blog Front Page and Blog Post, carry that grid as their body.

Each of those was a single tool call with a JSON payload. The server validated it, Umbraco saved it, and ModelsBuilder wrote strongly typed C# classes to disk before the next call returned.

Then the content

With the schema in place, the posts themselves are just more JSON: a layout that says which block goes where, the content data for each block and an expose list so Umbraco knows the blocks are live. The images were imported from local files into a media folder, then referenced by key from the hero and image blocks.

What surprised me

  • Read it back. Block payloads fail quietly if the keys do not line up, so the habit of fetching a document right after writing it paid for itself immediately.
  • Whole-object updates. Updating a document type means sending every field. Forget one and it is gone. Get, merge, update.
  • Parallelism has limits. Nine simultaneous writes against a SQLite development database produced table locks. Two or three at a time was smooth.

The Razor came last

All verified. The blog is live and every check passed.

**What I built**

- **Content model, all over MCP.** Five element types in the Blocks folder (Hero, Rich Text, Image, Quote, Blog Post List), one Block Grid data type named Blog Block Grid with per-block column span options, and two page types in the Pages folder: Blog Front Page and Blog Post. Site Root now allows Blog Front Page as a child, and Blog Front Page allows Blog Post. Each page type has its own template set as default. The data type was filed under /Custom/Umbraco.BlockGrid by the project's handler, as rule 3 expects.
- **Media.** A Blog folder in the media library with five Unsplash photos imported from the local folder: code on screen, network lines, puzzle hands, USB cables, connected structure.
- **Content.** A "Blog" front page under WWW with the root domain `/` assigned, carrying a Hero block and a Blog Post List block. Two published posts beneath it, "Why MCP is awesome: one protocol, every tool" and "Building this blog through MCP, without opening the backoffice". Both use rich text, quote and image blocks, including two images side by side at six columns each and a quote at eight columns to exercise the grid.
- **Rendering, following the AGENTS.md pipeline.** Templates call Umbraco's own block grid renderer. Each block has an adapter partial in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/` that maps to a plain model in `Models/Blocks/` and invokes a ViewComponent in `ViewComponents/`. All markup lives in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`. A shared layout, Tailwind styles for the grid and rich text, and the built `dist/` assets round it out. uSync exported everything.

**How to view it**

Umbraco is running in the background from my `dotnet run`. Open these:

```
https://localhost:44317/
https://localhost:44317/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-protocol-every-tool/
https://localhost:44317/building-this-blog-through-mcp-without-opening-the-backoffice/
```

Backoffice is at `/umbraco` with the scaffold's admin credentials.

**Verification results**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Front page and both posts | HTTP 200, zero "Could not render component" fallbacks |
| Column spans in rendered HTML | Match the saved layouts (12/12/6/6/12 and 12/12/12/8) |
| Cropped image URL from GetCropUrl | HTTP 200, image/jpeg |
| Umbraco log after requests | No errors |

**Things to know**

- **Nothing is broken**, but I only verified the HTML and image responses with curl. I did not take a screenshot, so the visual layout is unchecked by eye.
- **Compiled views need a rebuild.** Editing a `.cshtml` did not take effect on the running site, so every Razor change needs stop, build, start. The first attempt failed with a layout path that the view engine could not resolve. Fixed by using the full `~/Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml` path.
- **Parallel MCP writes lock SQLite.** Nine concurrent writes produced "database table is locked" errors and one duplicate-alias retry. Two or three writes at a time was reliable.
- **A loose log file.** My `dotnet run` output goes to `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/umbraco-run.log`. The running process holds it open, so delete it after stopping the site.
- **The post list adapter queries content.** The Blog Post List adapter reads the current page's children to build its plain model. That is still adapter mapping with no markup, but it is the one adapter that does more than copy fields.

- **The post list adapter queries content.** The Blog Post List adapter reads the current page's children to build its plain model. That is still adapter mapping with no markup, but it is the one adapter that does more than copy fields.
